title: Detection of Bluetooth-Based Data Exfiltration
summary: This strategy covers Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over Bluetooth, where data leaves a host over a short range wireless link to a nearby device that the attacker controls. It matters because Bluetooth traffic usually bypasses network monitoring entirely, so an air gapped or heavily segmented network can still leak data through a laptop that sits near a phone. The telemetry that makes it visible is endpoint Bluetooth service and driver events for adapter enablement, device pairing and bonding, operating system logs for incoming and outgoing file transfer over the personal area network profile, and network interface statistics on the Bluetooth adapter showing a transfer volume. It fails in practice because pairing is routine for headsets and phones, file transfer events are inconsistent across operating system versions, and most organisations collect no Bluetooth telemetry at all on endpoints.

beginner.definition: Bluetooth is a short range wireless link between devices, such as a laptop and a phone. This detection looks for a computer sending large amounts of data over that link. It also watches for new devices being paired to computers that should not be paired at all.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security monitoring watches the network cable and the internet connection. Bluetooth traffic does not use either, so it can carry data out unseen. A single paired phone can copy sensitive files from a protected machine. This matters most where networks are separated to keep data in.
howItWorks: The operating system records when the Bluetooth adapter is switched on, and when a new device is paired or trusted.
Bluetooth service logs record file transfers, including the personal area network profile used for networking.
A SIEM, which is a central system that collects and searches log events, gathers these events from the endpoints and looks for the pattern.
The rule checks whether the host is one where Bluetooth is prohibited or unused, such as a server or a secure workstation.
It then looks at the size and direction of the transfer, because a large outbound transfer is the interesting case.
A new pairing followed by a large outbound transfer on a restricted host raises the alert for the endpoint team.
beginner.example: Think of an office where every bag is checked at the door. A visitor who instead drops documents out of a window to a friend in the street has bypassed the check completely. Bluetooth is that window, and the pairing event is the moment the window is opened.
takeaways: Bluetooth exfiltration can leave a network with strong perimeter monitoring untouched.
The key combination is a new pairing on a host that should not pair, followed by a large outbound transfer.
Collect Bluetooth events on servers and sensitive workstations, because they are usually missing by default.

objectives: Explain why Bluetooth transfers evade network based data loss prevention controls.
Identify the endpoint and operating system events that record Bluetooth adapter, pairing and transfer activity.
Distinguish normal peripheral pairings from a pairing used to move data.
Correlate a new pairing event with transfer volume on the Bluetooth network interface.
Describe how to disable or restrict Bluetooth on host classes where it has no business purpose.
Explain the investigative limits of Bluetooth telemetry, including the lack of a remote device address in some logs.
dataSources: Windows Bluetooth service and driver events recording adapter state changes, device pairing and device removal
Windows event log entries for the Bluetooth file transfer and personal area network profiles with device name and transfer direction
macOS system log entries from the Bluetooth daemon recording pairing, connection and file push activity
Linux bluetooth daemon logs recording device pairing, bonding and object push transfers
Endpoint network interface counters for the Bluetooth adapter showing bytes sent and received over a connection session
logic: The pattern is a Bluetooth pairing or connection on a host where Bluetooth is not part of the normal baseline, followed by a large or sustained outbound transfer on the Bluetooth adapter. You correlate the pairing event, which carries the device name and sometimes the hardware address, with the adapter connection event for the same session, and with interface byte counters for the Bluetooth adapter over the same period. The malicious case shows a pairing with an unrecognised device name or a device that appears on several hosts, a transfer direction that is almost entirely outbound, and timing that follows access to sensitive files. The benign case is a user connecting a corporate headset, keyboard or mouse, where transfers are small in both directions and the device name is a known peripheral, usually repeated daily on the same laptop.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bluetooth Pairing Followed by Large Outbound Transfer
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventType:
#       - 'bluetooth_device_paired'
#       - 'bluetooth_file_transfer'
#   filter_peripherals:
#     DeviceName|contains:
#       - 'Headset'
#       - 'Mouse'
#       - 'Keyboard'
#   condition: selection and not filter_peripherals
# level: medium
falsePositives: Users pairing a corporate approved wireless headset or presentation clicker with a meeting room laptop
Field staff pairing a mobile phone for tethering, which produces a personal area network connection with substantial traffic
Asset tracking or inventory handhelds that connect to a workstation over Bluetooth during scheduled stock checks
Medical or laboratory instruments that transfer measurement files over Bluetooth to a nearby analysis computer
A user syncing a personal phone with a work laptop to copy photos or contacts, which is allowed by policy in some teams
tuningNotes: Start by inventorying which hosts even have a Bluetooth adapter, then scope the rule to servers, kiosks and secure workstations where Bluetooth is genuinely prohibited, because on general user laptops the peripheral noise is unmanageable. Baseline the device names and hardware addresses that appear legitimately per host and filter on that baseline rather than on device type words, since attackers can name a device anything. Add the outbound byte volume as a second condition so pairing alone stays informational. The coverage you lose by scoping to restricted hosts is theft from ordinary user machines, which you can partly recover by alerting on any Bluetooth adapter being re-enabled after it was administratively disabled.
